Adult individuals of Aequiyoldia eightsii reach a maximum shell length of 4.3 cm [Li = 4.3 cm], placing them among the medium-sized bivalves typical of Antarctic soft-sediment communities. This ultimate size is attained over a considerable period given the chronically low temperatures of their habitat. Growth in these waters proceeds at an exceptionally slow pace, and the maximum recorded lifespan approaches 43,800 days [am = 43,800 days] when the animals are maintained under the ambient thermal regime of approximately 2 °C [T = approximately 2 °C]. Such extreme longevity is a common feature among polar invertebrates, reflecting reduced metabolic demands and delayed senescence in cold environments. The onset of reproductive capacity occurs at a shell length of 2 cm [Lp = 2 cm], a threshold that corresponds roughly to one-third of the species' maximum linear dimension. This size at puberty, established through comparative analysis with the well-studied temperate clam Mya arenaria, implies that individuals must undergo a substantial period of somatic growth before initiating gametogenesis. Field surveys from nearshore habitats indicate that sexually mature specimens are most abundant in fine-grained sediments with moderate organic content, where local conditions appear to favour sustained growth and survival.

The planktonic larvae of Aequiyoldia eightsii undergo a critical developmental transition at a remarkably small size, with metamorphosis initiating at a shell length of just 0.075 cm . This measurement corresponds to the moment when the planktotrophic veliger larva loses its velum and begins the dramatic reorganisation of its body plan to adopt a benthic lifestyle. Achieving this size marks the conclusion of the larval dispersal phase and the onset of settlement onto suitable substrata, typically in subtidal muddy environments. Newly settled spat then devote the ensuing months to rapid shell accretion, gradually increasing their mass and gill surface area to support more efficient filter feeding. The dry tissue weight of an adult nearing its maximum shell length has been estimated at 0.474 grams , a value derived from size-corrected allometric relationships developed for functionally analogous species like Macoma baltica. This level of tissue mass suggests that the species invests heavily in somatic structure before shifting priorities toward reproductive effort, a pattern consistent with the iteroparous, long-lived life history strategy observed in many Antarctic molluscs.

Reproductive output in Aequiyoldia eightsii is characterised by a moderate fecundity relative to other polar bivalves, with females spawning approximately 4000 eggs per reproductive cycle [N_R_i = approximately 4000 eggs per reproductive cycle] when measured at a controlled water temperature of 2 °C [T = 2 °C]. Each female typically completes two spawning cycles per year [F_R_i = two spawning cycles per year], resulting in a substantial annual investment in offspring production. This dual spawning strategy, inferred from histological analysis of gonad condition over successive seasons, likely buffers against the high rates of larval mortality encountered during the extended planktonic development period in cold waters. The eggs themselves are relatively large, with an average diameter of 94 µm, and the wet weight at birth has been calculated at 0.00000029 grams [Wwb = 0.00000029 grams], reflecting a considerable allocation of maternal resources to each individual zygote. This substantial per-offspring investment contrasts sharply with the small egg sizes typical of temperate bivalves and is interpreted as an adaptation to the low food availability and slow growth rates that characterise the Southern Ocean environment.

Growth trajectories reconstructed from shell microgrowth bands reveal that Aequiyoldia eightsii requires decades to approach its asymptotic dimensions, with the oldest documented individuals persisting for 43,800 days [am = 43,800 days] at a temperature of 2 °C [T = 2 °C]. This extraordinary lifespan, recorded in specimens from the Ross Sea at a stable temperature of 2 °C [T = 2 °C], is among the highest reported for any infaunal bivalve and is thought to arise from a combination of low predation pressure, reduced metabolic costs, and the absence of catastrophic mortality events in the deep polar benthos. The species' ultimate dry weight of 0.474 grams  represents the culmination of this prolonged growth phase, after which somatic expansion essentially ceases and all surplus energy can be directed toward gamete production. Comparative studies with congeneric species from sub-Antarctic zones indicate that the extreme longevity of A. eightsii is coupled with a low annual reproductive turnover, a trade-off that appears to be conserved across the genus.

First reproduction in Aequiyoldia eightsii occurs when an individual attains a shell length of 2 cm [Lp = 2 cm], a size that in the field typically corresponds to an age of several decades under the prevailing approximately 2 °C [T = approximately 2 °C] conditions. This threshold for puberty was determined by gonad inspection of size-graded collections and aligns well with the relative length-to-maturity ratio established for the temperate clam Mya arenaria. Achieving this shell length marks a critical shift in life history priorities, transitioning from an exclusively somatic growth phase to one that includes substantial reproductive investment. The wet weight of a newly hatched larva, derived from the measured egg diameter of 94 µm, is 0.00000029 grams [Wwb = 0.00000029 grams], indicating that the species begins life with a considerable yolk reserve that supports the lecithotrophic early development stage. This large egg size likely enhances early survival in the oligotrophic waters of the Southern Ocean, where newly feeding larvae must quickly encounter sufficient phytoplankton to sustain their growth through the planktotrophic phase leading up to the metamorphic size of 0.075 cm . The life cycle of A. eightsii, from the 0.00000029 grams [Wwb = 0.00000029 grams] larval stage through to the 4.3 cm [Li = 4.3 cm] adult, exemplifies a strategy of slow growth, substantial maternal investment, and delayed reproduction that is finely tuned to the persistent cold and low productivity of Antarctic shelf ecosystems.
